cues.say: Component 3: Stateless API, one service. Each copy of your backend forgets the user between requests. Carts, orders and logins live in the database, so any copy can serve any request. You'll bring this up during version one, when you draw the basic design.
Think of it as: Bank tellers: any teller can help you, because your account is in the bank's system, not in one teller's head. Use it for every design, and scaling by adding copies.
Here's a real scenario. The pizza shop goes from 2 copies to 8 an hour before kickoff.
Without it: The cart lives in copy 1's memory.
The customer is stuck on copy 1; new copies sit idle.
Copy 1 crashes: the cart is gone.
With it: Copy 1 saves the cart to the database.
The next click lands on copy 5, which reads it back.
Why it works: Stateless copies are interchangeable, so more copies means more capacity.
In the interview, say: One service, run as several identical copies. Stateless, so I scale by adding copies.
A few related terms you may hear.
Monolith: One program deployed as a unit. Right for a small team.
Microservices: Many small programs calling each other. For big orgs.
Managed containers: The cloud runs copies of your packaged app (Cloud Run, ECS, Container Apps).
Kubernetes: Your own cluster for that. Needs people to run it.
Serverless: Code that runs once per event. Fine for small glue.
